name: Viognier

lines.s10: Viognier is the perfumed white of Condrieu in the northern Rhône: apricot, ripe peach and honeysuckle on a full, silky body.
lines.s20: Viognier comes from Condrieu, a short run of granite terraces above the Rhône. It smells of apricot, peach and honeysuckle, and it is dry and full, with a soft, almost oily feel and very little sharpness.
lines.s45: Viognier belongs to Condrieu, a short run of steep granite terraces above the Rhône, south of Lyon. It smells of apricot, ripe peach and honeysuckle. It is dry, full and silky, with gentle acidity and a warm finish. Most cellars use steel or older barrels, so the perfume stays in front. Condrieu tends to be the more restrained, while California and Australia are often riper and broader. Next door in Côte-Rôtie a little is fermented with Syrah to lift the red's scent. Pour it with lobster, roast chicken or a mild curry. By the 1960s it survived on only a few of those terraces.
lines.sale: Viognier gives you perfume and richness without sweetness: apricot and honeysuckle in a dry, silky white. I would pour it with the lobster, or for the guest who wants more scent than Chardonnay offers.

glass.lead: Apricot, ripe peach and honeysuckle on a full, oily frame, with low acidity and a warm finish.

ladder.where: Condrieu and Château-Grillet, Virginia, the Eden Valley
The Languedoc, California's Central Coast, the Swartland and Paarl

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity low to medium, alcohol high, body full, with an oily, glycerol texture.

old.where: Condrieu and Château-Grillet in the northern Rhône; the Languedoc
old.glass: Condrieu tends to be perfumed but poised: apricot, white peach and violet with a stony, faintly bitter finish, full bodied and low in acidity. Languedoc wines are usually lighter and simpler.
old.cellar: Usually dry and bottled alone; fermented in steel or in barrel, a modest share of it new, and often rested on its lees for texture.

new.where: California's Central Coast, Virginia, the Eden Valley, South Africa
new.glass: Typically riper and broader: ripe apricot, mango and orange peel, with higher alcohol and rounder, sweeter seeming fruit. Vanilla from new oak sometimes shows. Virginia and the Eden Valley tend to be fresher.
new.cellar: Bottled under the grape's name. Often picked very ripe, fermented in steel or barrel, and sometimes blended with Marsanne and Roussanne or fermented with a red as Shiraz Viognier.

contrast.why: Viognier must hang late to find its perfume, so warm, sunny sites push sugar and alcohol up fast. Condrieu's granite slopes ripen it more slowly, and the appellation names the place, not the grape.
contrast.blur: Virginia, the Eden Valley and cooler Californian coasts make restrained wines scented with violet, and a hot year or generous new oak can make Condrieu rich and heady.
contrast.call: Violet, a stony, bitter edge and fruit held in check lean Condrieu; mango, vanilla and a hotter finish lean New World.

service.temp: 50 to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius: too cold and the perfume closes.
service.glass: A white wine glass with a generous bowl; a Burgundy bowl for a rich Condrieu.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; pour it and let it warm a little in the glass.
service.age: Most within two to five years: it tires early, and the perfume is the first thing to fade.

with.why: a full, silky white for sweet, rich shellfish

with.dish: Roast chicken with apricots or tarragon
with.why: weight for the bird, perfume to lift it

with.dish: Mild, fragrant curry or a tagine
with.why: low acidity and perfume suit gentle spice
body to meet the butter and the sweet shellfish

labels.means: The northern Rhône appellation for Viognier alone; the label names the place, not the grape.
A tiny appellation of its own inside the Condrieu zone, a single granite amphitheatre of Viognier.
A red wine: Shiraz fermented with a little Viognier, in the manner of Côte-Rôtie.
A varietal wine from the Languedoc: lighter, simpler and made to be enjoyed young.

guest.a: Nearly always dry. The apricot and honeysuckle smell sweet, and the low acidity and full body feel rich, but there is very little sugar in the glass.

guest.q: I usually order Chardonnay. Will I like this?
guest.a: Very likely. It has the same weight and soft texture with far more perfume: apricot and honeysuckle where Chardonnay has apple and cream.

guest.q: Why is there a white grape in my red Côte-Rôtie?
guest.a: A little Viognier, up to a fifth by law and usually far less, is fermented in the vat with the Syrah. It lifts the perfume and helps to fix the colour.

compare.tell: Gewürztraminer is lychee and rose petal, with a spicier and often off dry finish; Viognier is apricot and honeysuckle, and nearly always dry.
Oaked Chardonnay has more acidity and no perfume of its own; Viognier is headier, with apricot and honeysuckle, and softer in acidity.
Marsanne is quieter and nuttier, with pear, almond and beeswax; Viognier is the loud one, all apricot and honeysuckle.

cards.front: Viognier: which two northern Rhône appellations are made from it alone?
cards.back: Condrieu and Château-Grillet, on granite terraces just south of Côte-Rôtie. Château-Grillet is a single estate with its own appellation inside the Condrieu zone.

cards.front: Viognier blind: Condrieu or the New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Violet, a stony, faintly bitter edge and fruit held in check lean Condrieu. Mango, vanilla from new oak and a hotter finish lean California or Australia.

cards.front: How much Viognier may Côte-Rôtie hold, and how is it added?
cards.back: Up to 20 per cent, though most wines carry far less. It is fermented in the vat with the Syrah, never blended in afterwards.

questions.q: A blind white is deep lemon, dry and full, with mango, ripe apricot and vanilla, low acidity and a hot finish. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Mango, vanilla from new oak and high alcohol on low acidity point to a warm New World Viognier. Condrieu tends to show violet and a stony restraint, with any oak held in the background.

questions.q: A guest who loves rich Chardonnay asks for something more perfumed, but still dry and full bodied. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Condrieu is Viognier: dry and full like a rich Chardonnay, with a perfume of apricot and honeysuckle. Moscato d'Asti is perfumed too, but it is sweet, light and gently sparkling.

questions.q: A guest reads that her red Côte-Rôtie holds a little white grape and asks which one it is. What do you tell her?
questions.exp: Côte-Rôtie may ferment up to 20 per cent Viognier with its Syrah. Marsanne and Roussanne are the white grapes allowed in red Hermitage and Saint-Joseph, not in Côte-Rôtie.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it: Condrieu and the Languedoc against California, Virginia, the Eden Valley and South Africa.

No Codex record on Viognier is believed wrong. The entry keeps TASTE.age (two to five years, it tires early) although Condrieu's own rule calls it a wine for keeping: Inter Rhône itself says two or three years, and the reviewed record stands.
The ladder has two rungs, moderate and warm, because the Codex holds Viognier as a warm climate grape with no true cool home.
The decline of the 1960s is told without a figure of area (the house rule on hectares); it stands on the Codex's own Rhône record and on The Oxford Companion to Wine.

Côte-Rôtie's limit of 20 per cent, Virginia's choice of Viognier as its signature grape in 2011 and the Rhône planters of the Central Coast stand on the Codex's own region records. The kinship of Viognier with Mondeuse Blanche and so with Syrah was left out: no primary source was read for it.
Château-Grillet is named as an appellation, which it is, though one estate holds the whole of it; a checker who reads it as a producer may strike the label row and the card's second sentence.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
